title: Count Ways to Build Rooms in an Ant Colony
statement:
An ant colony will have `n` rooms, labelled `0` to `n - 1`. The plan is the array `prevRoom` of length `n`: for every room `i` other than 0, room `prevRoom[i]` has to exist before room `i` can be built, and the two are joined directly. Room 0 already stands, so `prevRoom[0] = -1`, and the plan is such that, after everything is built, every room can be reached from room 0.

Rooms are built one after another, and a room may be built at any moment once its `prevRoom` exists. Count the distinct orders in which all the rooms can be built (every order starts with room 0) and return that count modulo `10^9 + 7`.
constraints: 0 <= prevRoom[i] < n for every 1 <= i < n
Once all rooms are built, every room is reachable from room 0
notes:
## Intuition

The plan is a tree rooted at room 0, and a valid build order is a topological order of it: every room comes after its parent. Trying all orders (the brute force walks through sets of built rooms) explodes quickly. Instead count with combinatorics. Shuffle all `n` rooms at random. An order is valid exactly when every room comes first among the rooms of its own subtree, and for a subtree of size `s` that happens with probability `1/s`, independently for different rooms. So the number of valid orders is

`n! / (size(0) · size(1) · ... · size(n - 1))`.

The same formula falls out of the tree DP that interleaves the children's orders with binomial coefficients.

## Approach

1. Build the `children` lists from `prevRoom`.
2. Run a breadth-first pass from room 0 to get `order`, in which every parent appears before its children.
3. Walk `order` backwards, so each room is finished before its parent: add `size[room]` to its parent, multiply `size[room]` into `sizeProduct`, and multiply `k + 1` into `factorial`, which ends as `n!`.
4. Division modulo the prime `10^9 + 7` is multiplication by the inverse, `sizeProduct^(MOD - 2)` by Fermat's little theorem; `power` computes it by repeated squaring.
5. Return `factorial` times that inverse, modulo `MOD`.

## Example 1, step by step

`prevRoom = [-1,0,1]` is the chain 0 → 1 → 2, so `order = [0, 1, 2]`. Backwards: room 2 has size 1 and makes `size[1] = 2`; room 1 has size 2 and makes `size[0] = 3`; room 0 has size 3. `sizeProduct = 1 · 2 · 3 = 6` and `factorial = 3! = 6`, so the answer is `6 / 6 = 1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + log MOD): one pass to build lists, one breadth-first pass, one backward pass and one modular power.
- Space: O(n) for `children`, `order` and `size`.

## Pitfalls

- Products of two values near `10^9` exceed 2^53, so plain JavaScript numbers lose precision; use `BigInt` (or 64-bit integers in Java and C).
- A recursive DFS can overflow the stack on a chain of `10^5` rooms; the breadth-first order avoids recursion.
- Room labels need not follow the tree: a child may have a smaller label than its parent, so do not assume `prevRoom[i] < i`.
- Never divide before taking the inverse: `n! mod p` is not divisible by `sizeProduct mod p` in ordinary arithmetic.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `children` | rooms whose `prevRoom` is the given room |
| `order` | rooms in breadth-first order from room 0 |
| `size` | number of rooms in each room's subtree |
| `sizeProduct` | product of all subtree sizes, modulo `MOD` |
| `factorial` | `n!` modulo `MOD`, built during the same loop |
| `power` | modular exponentiation used for the inverse |

narration.2: Every product is reduced modulo the prime 10^9 + 7; BigInt keeps the products exact.

narration.6: When the lowest bit of the exponent is set, multiply this power of base into the result.
narration.7: Square the base for the next bit.

narration.19: Breadth-first order starts at room 0, which is already built.
narration.20: Walk the queue; every room is appended after its parent.
narration.21: Append the children of the current room.
narration.27: Walk the order backwards so each subtree is complete before its root is handled.
narration.29: Add this room's finished subtree size to its parent's size.
narration.30: Multiply the subtree size into the denominator n! / (product of sizes).
narration.31: Meanwhile build n! one factor at a time.
narration.33: Divide by multiplying with the inverse sizeProduct^(MOD - 2) (Fermat) and return the count.
